content.thinking:
I need a root joint for parts without bones, which is straightforward. Now I'm thinking through the design: Genshin Impact-style cel-shading with a bright palette, gold filigree, tassels, and elemental glow motifs, centered around an alchemist's workbench prop sized realistically at about 1.8m wide.

I'm sketching the full layout: a bench with a raised back hutch holding bottle shelves and hanging herbs, roughly 1.9m wide and 1.95m tall overall. I'm working out precise coordinates for the tabletop, legs, stretcher shelf with crates and barrels, apron with gold trim, drawers with brass knobs on one side, an open shelf with jars on the other, and the hutch posts and shelf boards rising behind it.

Now I'm detailing the hutch's upper portion: a painted back panel with a parchment-style element chart, a curved scalloped crown beam in a Liyue-inspired gold-trimmed style, two shelves for bottles and books, and a hanging rail where herb bundles and tassels dangle in front of the shelves.

Resolving the viewer orientation — confirming that with the camera at +Z facing -Z, the model's right corresponds to +X, so I'll place items with that convention. On the left side I'll put a stack of varied-color books with gold trim, plus an open book on a small lectern stand.

In the center I'm placing the brass balance scale as the signature item, with a pillar, beam, chain-hung pans holding herbs or a gem, and a row of small weights at its base. Just right of that, I'm adding an alembic-style distillation apparatus with a glowing liquid flask over a brass burner, connected by a glass tube to a second flask, giving it that Sumeru-alchemy feel. Finally, I'm lining up a row of potion bottles with corks, wax seals, and labels in pyro, hydro, dendro, electro, and cryo colors.

Since true glass transparency isn't practical, I've decided to make each bottle's body use a flat glowing color for the liquid itself, with a white highlight strip and darker rim to suggest form, plus gold cap bands for detail -- keeping the glow strength moderate so the cel-shaded look still reads.

Then I'm thinking the bottle shape should split into two lathe sections: a lower glowing liquid portion up to a visible level line, and a pale glass-tinted upper portion above it, with a thin ring at the liquid surface to sell the effect. Next I'm planning the mortar and pestle piece with crushed herbs, positioned slightly forward of center.

For the herb details I'm envisioning potted dendro plants with leaf cards, twine-tied dried bundles, and a mushroom basket, pulling leaf textures reminiscent of silvermoon-style flora like Sweet Flower, Glaze Lily, and Cecilia, with the Glaze Lily cards given a subtle glow. I'm also adding smaller props — a candle, inkwell with quill, scrolls, labeled spice jars, keys, and considering a small bubbling green cauldron on the floor off to one side, weighing how far that pushes the composition's bounds.

I'm balancing the floor-level clutter by placing a tripod cauldron with fire logs to the left of the bench and a barrel, herb sacks, and crate to the right, plus a tasseled paper lantern hung from a bracket near the hutch. Under the shelf I'm adding crates of bottles, a basket, and drawer fronts stamped with gold plates and numbers, while the back wall gets a parchment chart of original elemental sigils (flame, drop, leaf, bolt, snowflake, swirl, diamond) alongside pinned notes, finished off with gold filigree decals and trim strips plus hanging tassels at the hutch corners.

I'm also considering a few floating glowing motes and a sparkle-touched sigil above the alembic for magical flair, while keeping everything else grounded to the floor, and working out wood cel-shading paints with grain streaks oriented differently per board axis, plus deciding on a 2048 or 4096 paint atlas size for adequate texel density given the scene's detail.

Running the texel math confirms 2048 gives roughly 3mm resolution versus 1024's 6.4mm, so I'm settling on 2048. For color budget, I'm keeping flat colors reserved mainly for potion liquids, flames, and glow effects while using cel paints for most surfaces including a stylized gold trim with bright yellow lit tones and a warm shadow tone to get that cel-shaded metal look seen in Genshin-style art.

Since everything attaches to a single root joint, merging repeated geometry is purely about reducing part count rather than bone grouping. I'm sketching a small helper function that wraps the builder's part call, defaulting the bone to root so I don't have to repeat that for every box or shape I create.

Now I'm defining helpers for boxes, cylinders, and lathe shapes to generate the workbench geometry, plus planning textures (svg labels, book spines, drawer filigree, glowing flame cards) before laying out the actual coordinates for the bench top and surrounding furniture pieces.

For the top, I'm positioning it with a plank paint function that adds seams every 0.14m along the x-axis, wrapped in a cel shader so the top surface reads lit while the sides fall into shadow, then adding a gold trim inlay strip along the front edge for detail.

Now I'm sketching the apron and drawer cabinet: an apron board under the top, then a right-side cabinet block with stacked drawer fronts featuring gold filigree plates and ring-pull knobs, while the left side stays open with a lower shelf—though I'm reconsidering the cabinet's exact x-range to fit the proportions better.

Revising this into a full-height right-side cabinet from floor to apron with two upper drawers and a lower cupboard door (ornate handle, gold filigree panel, plinth base), while the left side becomes open with front and back legs, a lower shelf holding a jar, basket, crate of bottles, and sack.

Still placing legs and rails...

Still placing hutch shelves...

Now for the crown, I'm shaping a curved canopy roof reminiscent of Chinese eaves, extruding a flattened curve profile across the width and centering its depth along z.

Adding teal tile roof with gold fascia trim, ridge detailing, and dangling tassels plus a hanging lantern, then adjusting overall height so the crown sits around 2m by tweaking post, shelf, and roof levels for proportion.

For the hanging rail, I'm placing a rod near y=1.82 suspended from hooks under the roof rather than resting on posts, with herb bundles and cards dangling down to partially overlap the upper shelf's stored items around 1.5-1.8m.

Mid shelf gets potion bottles and jars, while the bench top below becomes the main workspace — I'm placing taller items like the alembic out front where the shelf doesn't block clearance, keeping items near the back panel short enough to fit under the lower shelf.

Now I'm planning the shelf heights (lower shelf at 1.3 giving 0.4m clearance, upper shelf at 1.6, posts to 1.92, roof above) and starting to lay out items across the 1.9m-wide table: a book stack and lectern with an open grimoire near the left end.

I'm placing an open book on a stand at one spot, a stack of closed books further along with an inkwell and quill on top, then moving to the center of the table where I'm positioning a scale with weights and a mortar nearby.

On the right side I'm planning out an alembic apparatus: a tripod burner holding a glowing green flask, with a curved condenser tube leading to a collecting bottle, checking that its placement doesn't overlap the scale.

Then I'm laying out the front right potion row with small bottles plus a tall one, a potted plant further right, and a mushroom basket nearby. Along the back panel I'm placing a row of five corked jars holding herbs and pearls.

For floor items I'm designing a cauldron on three stubby legs at the far left, with a glowing green liquid disc on top and a soft flame glow beneath it, sitting over a small stone brazier rather than a full fire pit to keep things simple.

On the right side I'm placing a barrel with gold hoops, plus a sack of herbs and a crate of flasks, skipping extras like a broom. I'm debating whether to add a patterned rug under the bench for color but leaning toward skipping it to avoid unnecessary complexity.

Rug sits centered on the floor with items' bottoms slightly sinking into its top surface, which is fine visually since the rug is a solid box. Now I'm cataloging the textures I'll need: the rug, wall chart, potion labels, drawer and door filigree plates, book spines, open grimoire pages with runes, leaf cards, a tassel, a curtain or banner, a paper lantern, and a scroll.

I'm keeping atlas sizes modest to avoid bloat, then settling on a bright Genshin-style palette — warm wood tones with a dark wood accent, teal highlights, cream, gold, red lacquer, and stone grey — to define as color constants before writing the generation code.

Adding elemental glow colors...

Now I'm planning the helper functions for the workbench file, deciding to lean on THREE geometries like lathe shapes for turned items, keeping segment counts low for small props. I'm setting up a typed part-creation helper and figuring out how to properly type its options object.

Since referencing the builder at module scope is awkward, I'll keep everything inside the build function with closures instead of splitting into separate functions. For rotations I'll use degree values on the XYZ axes, box geometry for flat-shaded cel look, and now I'm defining wood paint materials for the props.

Writing plank seam logic...

Adding tile ridge lines...

Reconsidering the roof shape entirely—maybe a lathe-based pagoda-style hip roof with four segments would look better than extrusion, though I'd need to scale it to fit the rectangular footprint rather than a square one.

Working out the roof box dimensions, I need to figure out how a 4-segment lathe spin affects corner placement—whether corners land on the diagonal or axes—then derive the scale factors to hit a target half-width and half-depth, using radius 0.9 as a reference to compute the needed x and z scaling.

I'm now considering an alternative: instead of a tapered lathe pyramid (which degenerates oddly into a pointed tent shape), building the roof as an extruded gable profile in the side view, with a curved pagoda-style section sloping concave from a ridge point down to the eave tips.

This gives me a long barrel roof with flat gable ends spanning the full x-length, plus I want to add gold ornamental caps at the gable ends, tile lines running along the extrusion direction, a gold ridge cap tube with small finials at each end, and upturned corners for the pagoda effect.

I'll leave the gable face decoration simple for now and revisit with an overlay if needed. Time to move on to writing all the actual build code efficiently, starting with constants and the rug geometry with its border and textured top plane.

For the rug texture, I'm sketching an SVG with teal and cream borders, a gold pattern, and a central medallion with tassel fringe, sized for decent resolution. I need to watch for z-fighting since the plane sits only half a millimeter above the rug box top.

I'm fixing the floor baseline by introducing a constant F=0.012 so all floor items — rug, bench legs, etc. — sit consistently above the rug surface, then starting to lay out the bench pieces with absolute coordinates beginning with the top slab.

Now I'm adding the gold inlay trim along the bench's front edge and sketching small gold corner caps at the four corners to accent the design.

I'm thinking about adding a decorative runner across the top surface—a flat teal cloth with gold trim, implemented as either a thin box or simply a textured plane positioned just above the tabletop so items can sit on it naturally. Then I'm moving on to work out the structure of the left legs.

Now I'm detailing the leg geometry with posts and gold foot caps, then shifting to the cabinet: a dark wood frame sitting on a plinth, with a front face holding two stacked drawer panels in lighter wood.

Each drawer gets a decorative gold filigree plate near a ring-pull handle, and below them I'm adding a cupboard door panel filled with a larger filigree decal, small gold hinge boxes, and a vertical bar-and-ball handle -- considering whether to split it into a double door setup.

Now I'm placing the lower shelf with crates, baskets, and a jar on top, and sketching a back panel under the top-left section for added depth.

For the lower stretcher rails, I'm positioning front and side rails with gold inlay details, adding small gold spheres as studs along the front rail, and designing scrolled corner brackets at each leg-rail joint for decorative reinforcement.

Now moving to the hutch: I'm placing posts at either side, considering Genshin Liyue-inspired aesthetics with red lacquer and gold trim to contrast the natural wood of the bench below, possibly adding gold ring bands along the posts for extra ornamentation.

For the backdrop, I'm planning a cream plaster back panel with subtle plank texturing, and adding wall decor like a hanging scroll in the visible gap between the shelves to balance the composition against the busy foreground items.

I'm also sketching in smaller hanging elements -- a parchment chart, a pinned note, and tools like a ladle and tongs hung on hooks -- then placing a larger alchemical transmutation circle emblem higher up on the panel with a glowing effect to anchor the overall scene.

I'll add scroll brackets beneath the shelves, then populate the upper shelf with standing books on the left, a glowing crystal on a stand at center, and jars with herbs plus an hourglass on the right. The mid shelf gets a row of elemental potion bottles with labels and tassels spaced evenly across, alongside a small vial rack.

Designing potion lathe profiles...

I could add a darker foot ring at the base for shading, then build the body shape using a vertical sweep with a radius profile, applying different sector colors for highlight and shadow strips to break up the flat emissive glow.

With about 15 potions needing roughly 8 parts each, that's around 120 parts total, well within the 1000-part budget. For labels, I'll use small decal planes with a texture applied, positioned on the bottle surface.

A flat plane label on a curved body risks sinking into the surface at the edges due to curvature, so instead I'll use a conforming decal function that follows the part's surface shape, placed at the front tangent point with proper direction and sizing.

Now I'm planning the seven element label textures — each a parchment-style rounded rect with an ink border and a colored glyph symbol (flame, drop, leaf, bolt, snow, swirl, diamond) rendered small to keep texture atlas usage low, using reduced segment count on the decals to save on triangle count.

Still defining glyph paths... Now I'm planning potion bottle shapes using lathe profiles -- round flasks, tall vials, boxy bottles, teardrop gems, and gourd-like double spheres, each with its own geometry.

For the cork and finishing touches, I'm adding a cone cap with gold or wax-seal coloring, plus hanging tassel cards made from frames with gold thread and beads, collecting all the frame arrays so I can batch them into single card-draw calls at the end.

Now I'm sketching out the brass balance scale: a stepped lathe base, a thin pillar, and a top bracket beam with tapered rod ends, small decorative spheres, and a vertical pointer needle running from the beam's center down toward a scale plate — with pans still needing to be hung.

For the pans, I'm planning thin chain rods connecting the beam ends to the pan rims, with wide shallow gold bowl pans—one holding glowing gem crystals, the other holding herbs and weights—and tilting the beam slightly (about 6°) so one side sits lower to show the imbalance from the heavier contents, adjusting the endpoint heights accordingly.

I'm filling the left pan with stacked gold weights and a gem, the right pan with herb leaves and a small gem, plus a tray of graduated brass weights nearby. For the alembic, I'm building a tripod burner stand with an iron ring, a spirit lamp at its base, and a small glowing teardrop flame beneath the flask.

Now I'm shaping the glowing green liquid flask above the flame with a glass neck leading up, then adding the swan-neck condenser tube arching from the alembic head down to a small receiving bottle with glowing lime liquid.

I'm fine-tuning the positions so the receiving bottle and tube end align properly and stay within the pan boundaries, nudging the whole alembic assembly slightly right to avoid overlap.

For the glass tubes, I'm giving them a pale blue-white tint with a highlight to suggest glass without full transparency, and considering tiny glowing motes above the receiving flask for visual interest. I'm also starting to lay out the mortar and pestle with a lathed stone bowl profile and a tilted capsule-shaped pestle resting across its rim.

Now I'm designing a closed book object: layered cover boards, an inset cream page block, a spine with gold banding, corner caps, and a decorative title plate texture, planning to reuse a few SVG cover textures with slight color variants.

For standing books on the shelf, I'm making simple boxes with spine-facing decals—thin planes positioned at the front face showing bands and title lines, generated via a seeded texture function to keep file sizes small across several spine variants. Then I'm moving on to the open grimoire resting on a small lectern stand.

For the lectern itself, I'm working out the geometry: a tilted reading board rotated about the x-axis so its surface faces up and toward the viewer, sitting on a simple base block with legs, positioning the board center and figuring out the rotation math so the normal correctly points toward +z.

Now I'm designing the lectern body as an extruded wedge shape with a sloped top at roughly 22 degrees, and planning the open book resting on that slope as two tilted page halves in a V shape with a leather cover underneath.

For visual flair I want to add magical touches: handwritten page texture with glowing rune diagrams, plus a small floating glowing rune circle hovering above the book as a double-sided billboard card so it reads from any angle.

Now I'm moving on to a potted plant: a lathe-turned teal and white ceramic pot with gold rim detailing, and leaf clusters arranged in a tilted ring pattern scattered around the soil to give it natural fullness.

For radial leaf arrangements, the flow direction should actually be tangential rather than purely outward, so the face normal aligns with the tangent of the circle while the blade still contains the radial-up axis. I'm leaning toward setting lean to zero and letting the flow vector itself handle the sideways orientation, though the droop effect might need a different tweak.

I like the idea of adding `cross:true` for leaf clusters and herb bundles so each leaf renders as two intersecting planes, making it look full from any viewing angle without much extra triangle cost—flow direction becomes irrelevant in that mode.

Now I'm sketching out the different leaf SVG types: a broad two-tone leaf with a highlighted vein, a pinnate fern frond, a flower sprig with glowing white-teal petals, a lavender spike with small purple buds, and a dried herb bundle texture resembling rosemary.

For hanging herb bundles, I'm reasoning through how the `lean 180` rotation flips the card's growth direction, so I need to draw each sprig upright (stem at bottom, leaves toward top) so that when it hangs upside down the orientation looks natural. I'm also planning bench herbs as upright bundles standing in a ceramic vase using crossed cards, plus a separate flat herb bundle lying on the table built from a few curved stem sweeps in green.

I'm sketching out a mushroom basket with striped woven paint and spotted mushroom caps, deciding where to place it near the barrel or on the bench, then adding five dried herb bundles hanging over the rail above. Finally I'm thinking through a candle setup—cream lathe candle with a wax drip, a glowing flame, and a gold holder—placed near the book stack, and working out how to fake a soft glow halo using a translucent radial-gradient disc.

An inkwell with teal glass and a feather quill made from a thin rod plus a feather card seems simple enough to add, and I'm considering tossing a few rolled scrolls with ribbon and gold caps into a floor tube by the cabinet, though I might skip some for time. I'm also planning a lantern hung from a wall bracket extending off the right post—a red paper lantern body with gold caps, tassel, and warm inner glow.

Now I'm laying out the floor scene: a cauldron on the left surrounded by a ring of stone boxes, three logs, and glowing orange-yellow flame cones, with the cauldron itself built as a lathed iron pot shape resting on three thin iron legs.

I'm adding the cauldron's glowing green liquid disc, rising bubble spheres, an arc-shaped handle, and small gold bands, plus a leaning stirring ladle propped against the pot rim, with steam wisps still to come.

Now I'm swapping steam for a swirling glowing green magic spiral tube above the cauldron. To the right I'm placing a lathed wooden barrel with iron hoops, and nearby a couple of tied burlap sacks with label tags.

I'm also adding a wooden crate with plank lines and gold corners holding small potion bottles and straw, positioned near the barrel on the bench's right side. Under the bench on the left I'm putting a corked jar, a few small bottles, a woven herb basket, and a stack of three books -- skipping the hanging key hook for now and moving on to floating glow motes.

For the glow motes I'm scattering roughly a dozen small glowing star-shaped sparkle cards near the scales and alembic, using just two tinted textures (gold and teal) rendered as vertical front-facing cards to keep things simple, and roughly estimating part counts across the bench, hutch, and shelf items.

I'm staying well under the colour budget by reusing flat cel paints for glass, cork, and leather, adding subtle mottled texture to the leather rather than new flat colours.

Now I'm reviewing how lathe outlines need to start from the axis and sweep around, with smoothing on sharp profile corners, then mapping out the exact function signatures I'll need for lathe, extrude, sweep, and rod operations before writing the actual construction code.

Still writing helper functions...

The part function has overloaded signatures, so grabbing a type from Parameters is risky since TypeScript picks the last overload. I should just check the actual part signature in the source to get the right options type.

input.command: grep -n "part(\|part:\|PartOptions\|export type Part" src/*.ts | head -30; grep -n "decal" src/*.ts | head
